hits.name: Armin Ronacher ⇌
hits.text:
A pretty common reply today is "the value is in the testsuite". I'm not sure if this is LLM slop or genuine replies, but you don't actually need a test suite to rebuild something. In fact, you're probably better off having the agent builds its own test suite specifically for porting if that's what you're after. In part because lots of pre-existing tests are bad for hill climbing.

An existing test-suite helps for sure, but I'm not at all convinced that it's necessary. For instance I had an agent a few weeks ago re-implement excel's formula engine and it build its own test suite from scratch.

hits.name: Peter Yang
hits.text:
I had a great chat with my friend @jacalulu (PM Director at Google Labs) about how Gemini 4 changed how Google builds products and how parents can get kids to explore AI.

Some takes I loved:

1. “It shouldn’t take someone longer to read your doc than it took you to write it.”

Writing is thinking. AI can be a thought partner, but you should firmly be in the driver’s seat.

2. “It’s no longer about can you build it, it’s about should it even exist?”

Code went from a scarce asset to basically free. If you can “throw a couple of agents at it over a weekend,” it’s probably not a durable product. So the hard part now is deciding what’s worth building in the first place.

3. “Why do you even want a person in your product?”

Agents do more of our work every month, so you should ask if your product needs a UI at all. Jaclyn thinks people will still show up to create, learn, or be entertained. Any task that feels like a chore should be built for agents first.

4. “Don’t just give users exactly what they want.”

Talk to them all the time, but find the root problem and solve it in a way they wouldn’t have thought of. You want them to walk away thinking, “I didn’t think this was possible, but it’s exactly what I wanted.”

5. “You shouldn’t expect users to know how to write elaborate prompts.”

Small business owners don’t have time to start from an empty prompt box. So her team built Pomelli, Google’s tool for SMBs to create on-brand content, to read your website and learn your business first.

6. “Let your kid be your creative director.”

Jaclyn’s 5-year-old loves scary stories, so they made their own podcast, Maya and the Fog. Her daughter picks the voices, names the characters, and gives notes on each cut, and Jaclyn has the agent produce the episode. It’s live on Spotify.

📌 Watch now: https://t.co/8hLt6x6atQ

hits.name: Kai
hits.text:
Anthropic added an invisible text watermark to Claude, though it is a lot less dramatic than people think.

The watermark attaches to words Claude picks on its own. Use it to fix grammar or typos in your own draft, and there is barely any signal left to detect.

Code is mostly unaffected too since syntax has to be exact. The mark shows up in longer prose, translations, and code comments.

It runs across all of Claude: web chat, the API, and Claude Code.

They rolled this out in August for the new EU AI rules. The December 2 date going around is the deadline to finish updating older models.

One catch: regular users cannot check their own text. Anthropic only gives the detector tool to regulators, media, and compliance teams right now.

trend_radar.legend: Trend match 0-100% = 1 - prod(1 - w) over matched 24 h keywords that another author also used in the 48 h window (w: rank 1-10 0.35, 11-25 0.22, 26-40 0.12, curated 0.20). Verdict: >= 50% -> trend; else video/image in the post data -> visual; else >= 100K followers (outsiders without follower data: >= 500K views, estimate) -> author/audience; else coincidence/other. Missing data shows as 'no data'. Heat = sum log10(views) of topic posts (24 h x1, 24-48 h x0.5), scaled to 100. Momentum = log-views last 24 h / previous 24 h. Trend-input-only accounts feed the corpus but are never shown as hits.
